stories.post_title: AITA for moving to the guest room because my husband’s "sleepmaxxing" routines are ruining my sleep?
stories.summary: A wife moves to the guest room after her husband's extreme 'sleepmaxxing' routine (a freezing room, a red-light panel, pink noise and a no-movement rule) leaves her unable to rest, angering him and his mother.

stories.post_title: Hot take - Kurt Cobain didn't shoot up right before he died, in fact, he died in withdrawal...
stories.summary: A Redditor theorizes that Kurt Cobain was in heroin withdrawal, not freshly high, when he died, and argues that harm reduction might have helped him more than an abstinence-only approach.

stories.post_title: I lost 8 hours in a thrift store basement and I still can't explain it
stories.summary: A man wanders into a thrift store's antique basement for what feels like 20 minutes, only to come back upstairs to police, his crying wife, and the news that 8 hours have passed.

facts.summary: Climbing a staircase 100 km to space means altitude sickness, the death zone, boiling-point limits, and the twist that you still feel about 97% of normal gravity at the top.
A week with no sleep escalates from foggy focus to microsleeps, hallucinations and paranoia, with the twist that your brain forces microsleeps anyway, so you can't fully stop sleeping.
A guy who can pause time uses it to sleep, study and binge, but keeps aging for twenty years, hits presbyopia around forty, and unpauses older than his teacher with the exam forgotten.

A stickman in a magic suit sinks into the Mariana Trench past doubling pressure, the end of sunlight, glowing animals and a snailfish to the nearly 11 km bottom, where the twist is that a plastic bag got there first.

If the Moon vanished, nights would get darker, tides would shrink to about a third, moonlight-timed coral spawning would lose its cue, total solar eclipses would end, and Earth's tilt could wobble far more over millions of years, with the twist that the Moon is already drifting away about 3.8 cm a year.

Your brain replays embarrassing moments for years because the amygdala and stress hormones stamp emotional events into memory, social pain overlaps with physical pain in the brain, and recalling a memory re-saves it, with the twist from the spotlight effect that far fewer people noticed than you think.

Drinking only coffee for 30 days is basically a starvation fast: caffeine blocks adenosine, glycogen runs out within about a day, intake past the roughly 400 mg limit brings a racing heart and no sleep, muscle breakdown and ketone breath follow, refeeding syndrome makes the first meal risky, and the twist is that coffee is about 98% water.

A guy who can read every mind for one day gets overwhelmed by unfiltered thoughts, learns minds wander about 47% of the time, that most thinking isn't even words, and that nearly everyone has earworms, with the twist that his crush is only wondering why he has stared at her all day.

Being stranded on a tiny Pacific island escalates from realizing the Pacific covers about 30% of Earth, to seawater being too salty to drink, coconut water hydrating but acting as a laxative, failed stick fire, and roughly three weeks without food, with the twist that after rescue nobody in the group chat noticed you were gone.

You can't tickle yourself because your cerebellum predicts the touch from your own movement and dampens it; a robot delay of 0.2 seconds brings the tickle back, and the same prediction makes people tap back about 40% harder, which is why play fights escalate.

Going without water escalates from smug at hour one, to thirst signaling about one percent water loss, foggy focus at two percent, thickened blood and a racing heart, to emergency mode near the roughly three-day survival limit, with the twist that about twenty percent of your water comes from food and watermelon is ninety-two percent water.

If you could never feel pain, as in congenital insensitivity to pain caused by a broken SCN9A gene, you'd ignore stubbed toes, hot pans, joint wear and hidden fractures, with the twist that the same gene usually erases your sense of smell too.

Lost in the Sahara with one water bottle, you learn it's mostly rocks, you can sweat over a liter an hour, mirages are bent skylight, rationing is a mistake and heat stroke starts past forty degrees, with the twist that an army survival table shows one bottle barely changes the roughly two-day survival time at forty-nine degrees.

facts.topic: why time speeds up with age
facts.summary: Time seems to speed up with age because each year is a smaller fraction of your life, and routine leaves fewer new memories, so the brain judges past time as shorter (the holiday paradox), with the twist that adding new 'firsts' makes time feel longer.

Spending an Antarctic winter with no heat brings months of polar night, minus-forty frostbite, desert dryness, hypothermia below 35°C and Vostok's record minus 89.2°C, with the twist that male emperor penguins survive the same winter fasting in huddles that can top 20°C inside.

A guy who can teleport only 10 meters at a time uses it for snacks and a 1,000-blink commute, then learns that blinking upward means falling at about 50 km/h and that teleporting keeps his speed, so repeated blinks push him toward roughly 200 km/h terminal velocity, with the twist that his fitness watch thinks he died.

Being swallowed by a whale only works with a sperm whale, since a blue whale can barely swallow a beach ball; inside there is no breathable air, a muscular first stomach that squeezes, and dives over two kilometers deep, with the twist that the famous 1891 sailor survival story was likely a hoax.

You feel stares because your eyes and brain are built to detect gaze, your side vision catches heads turning, and your brain defaults to assuming you're being watched, but controlled tests show no sixth sense, with the twist from an 1898 observation that turning to check often makes people look at you, so you create the stare.

Sitting in a sauna that never turns off escalates from feeling fine in 90°C dry air, thanks to sweat and air being a poor heat conductor, to a heart rate near 150 bpm, dizziness, and heat stroke risk as core temperature nears 40°C, with a 1775 steak experiment and the twist that Finland has about three million saunas, yet even Finns step out to cool off in a lake.

Being permanently invisible starts out fun but leaves you blind because your retinas can't absorb light, puts your undigested lunch on display, and makes traffic and doorways a cartoon nightmare, with the twist that mosquitoes still find you by tracking the carbon dioxide in your breath.

long.summary: What happens if you jump into Jupiter? You blast through radiation, scorching entry, toxic freezing clouds, the depth where the Galileo probe went silent, and an ocean of metallic hydrogen, and you never land because Jupiter has no surface; the twist is that at the very center you weigh nothing.
